archetype.name: Cup Contender (puck-possession)
archetype.definition: A team that controls play at 5-on-5 as well as almost anyone in the league, with an A- forward group and a record that its underlying play supports, even if the finishing and special teams haven't caught up yet.

report.headline: Elite 5-on-5 control is carrying Tampa while the power play and finishing lag
report.take:
Tampa Bay is 6-2-0 and ninth on the site, but the record undersells how thoroughly it has run games. Its 58.9% expected-goals share at 5-on-5 is second in the league, its shot-attempt share is fourth, and it is putting 30.9 shots a game on net while allowing 22.8. That is a team that has the puck, gets to the dangerous areas and keeps opponents out of them. The forward group earns its A- grade. Brandon Hagel is second among 117 left wingers with 6 goals and 11 points, and Kucherov and Guentzel are right behind him. The bottom of the lineup is winning its minutes too: Cirelli's on-ice expected-goals share is 68.2%, and Goncalves is at 63.5% despite no points.

The goal column doesn't match the territory. Tampa ranks only 14th in goals a game. Its skaters shoot 10.1% in all situations, 24th in the league and below the league's 11.3%. The power play converts 10.7%, 30th of 32, on a roster that has posted power plays at 25% or better in three of the last five seasons. The two losses, both to the Rangers, were 1-5 and 1-4 games in which the offense simply didn't finish. The penalty kill at 75% has also bled goals.

There is a little good fortune on the other side of the ledger. Tampa's Pts vs Goal Diff of 1.7 ranks third, helped by a 4-3 overtime win over Seattle and a one-goal win over Minnesota. A goal differential of 4 doesn't fully earn a 6-2 start. The goaltending is a C: Vasilevskiy is at .886 with a slightly negative GSAx over six starts, and Hildeby has been better in two. On balance, finishing that is due to rise outweighs the close-game luck that is due to fall, because the shot share and chance share are what tend to hold.

The 123-point pace won't survive the season, and nobody should expect it to. But this looks like the same team that put up 106 points last year, with stronger 5-on-5 numbers than any of its last five seasons. Once the power play normalizes, the goals should follow the chances.

strengths.title: Owning the chances at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Tampa's expected-goals share is second in the league and well above any of its last five seasons. It outshoots opponents by a wide margin at both ends. A gap this large, backed by shot-attempt share as well, is the most stable thing in an eight-game sample.

strengths.title: Hagel leads a deep forward group
strengths.body: Hagel has 6 goals on 38 shots and ranks second at his position. Kucherov and Guentzel give the top six three point-a-game threats. Every regular forward is above 53% in on-ice expected goals, so the depth isn't being outplayed while the stars score.

strengths.title: Forwards held under expectation
strengths.body: Opposing forwards are scoring below their own averages against Tampa, sixth-best in the league. That fits a team allowing so few shots. Opposing wingers in particular have been kept quiet.

concerns.title: Power play and penalty kill underwater
concerns.body: The power play at 10.7% is 30th and the penalty kill at 75% is 22nd, both well below league average. This is a big break from Tampa's history, where the PK has held above 79% for five straight seasons. Expect real improvement, but special teams are the main reason the goal differential trails the 5-on-5 play.

concerns.title: Vasilevskiy's start is ordinary
concerns.body: The starter is at .886 with a GSAx of -0.4, and the team's goaltending grade is a C. Light shot volume against has hidden it so far. Against higher-shooting opponents, an average-or-worse goalie matters more.

concerns.title: Defensemen getting beaten for points
concerns.body: Opposing defensemen are scoring above expectation against Tampa, 21st in the league. They account for a bigger share of the points against than the league norm. It's a small leak in an otherwise tight structure, worth watching against puck-moving bluelines.

trend.note: After an opening loss to the Rangers, Tampa won four straight, dropped a second game to New York, then closed with two more wins. The last five games run slightly ahead of the season pace in both points percentage and scoring.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games against three of the West's best
weekAhead.body:
This is the hardest week of the young season: at Vegas, then a back-to-back at Colorado and Utah. All three sit in the site's top eight, and Vegas (8-2-0) has the league's best goal differential. Two of the three (Vegas and Colorado) carry PDOs well above 100, which suggests some of their scoring is running hot, while Tampa's possession game is the more repeatable product.

The swing is special teams. Vegas and Utah both have bottom-ten penalty kills, an opening for a Tampa power play due to wake up. But both also have top-five power plays, and Tampa's kill is the thing most likely to cost it a game. A split of the week would be a fine result; taking two of three would say a lot.

keyMatchups.title: Tampa's PK against Utah's power play
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts 35.3% on the power play, first in the league, and Vegas is fifth. Tampa's 75% kill has to tighten or stay out of the box. Of everything on this trip, this is where Tampa looks most exposed.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against shaky Colorado goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Colorado's goalies carry a C- grade and a GSAx of -2.7, propped up by a 106.8 PDO. Tampa's shot volume, third in the league, is exactly the pressure that can expose that. This is the likeliest game for Tampa's finishing to break out.

keyMatchups.title: Utah takes away the shots
keyMatchups.body: Utah allows 19.3 shots a game, fewest in the league, and has an A+ blueline. That makes it the first opponent that can match Tampa's possession game. It comes on the second night of a back-to-back.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the power play, 30th in the league, can cash in against the weak penalty kills of Vegas and Utah.

restOfSeason.body:
Tampa will not keep a 123-point pace. A goals-for-and-against record this modest, with close-game luck already banked, would normally point toward a cooler run. The process argues the other way. A team with the second-best expected-goals share and a top-six shots-against rate rarely keeps shooting near the league's bottom third, and a power play this talented won't stay at 10.7%. As finishing and special teams drift back toward Tampa's norms, the goal differential should widen even as the record slows to something like 100 to 110 points.

What's sustainable is the 5-on-5 control and the forward depth. What regresses is the close-game cushion and, in Tampa's favor, the shooting and power-play slumps. The open question is the crease: if Vasilevskiy stays near .886, Hildeby's two good starts become a real conversation, and the goaltending caps how high this team can finish.
swingFactors: Penalty kill against top power plays

confidence.note: Only 8 games, but the 5-on-5 numbers are strong and consistent with recent seasons.
